key_cases.case_name: Sheboygan County DHHS v. Julie A.B.
key_cases.holding: At the dispositional phase of a TPR the circuit court must treat the child's best interests as the prevailing factor, weighing the six Wis. Stat. sec. 48.426(3) factors and any others against that standard; applying a different standard (such as requiring 'egregious' unfitness) is an error of law.
key_cases.relevance: It is the controlling Wisconsin statement of the disposition standard governing every TPR and adoption outcome.
key_cases.quote: The best interests of the child is the polestar for the court in a dispositional hearing, and a failure to apply that standard is an error of law.

key_cases.holding: Wisconsin TPR proceeds in two phases: grounds/unfitness, which the petitioner must prove by clear and convincing evidence and where partial summary judgment is available when no material fact is disputed, followed by a dispositional phase governed by the child's best interests.
key_cases.relevance: It is the leading modern statement of Wisconsin's two-part TPR procedure and the gateway role of the unfitness finding.
key_cases.quote: A finding of parental unfitness is a necessary prerequisite to termination of parental rights, but a finding of unfitness does not necessitate that parental rights be terminated.

key_cases.holding: The 'failure to assume parental responsibility' ground is measured by a totality-of-the-circumstances test looking at the parent's conduct across the child's entire life, and may include exposing the child to a hazardous living environment.
key_cases.relevance: It supplies the governing test for one of the most frequently pleaded TPR grounds in Wisconsin.
key_cases.quote: We conclude that a fact-finder should consider a parent's actions throughout the entirety of the child's life when determining whether he has assumed parental responsibility.

key_cases.court: Supreme Court of the United States
key_cases.holding: Due process requires a State to support its allegations by at least clear and convincing evidence before it may sever completely and irrevocably the rights of parents in their natural child.
key_cases.relevance: It is the constitutional standard of proof underlying Wisconsin's TPR grounds phase.
key_cases.quote: The fundamental liberty interest of natural parents in the care, custody, and management of their child does not evaporate simply because they have not been model parents

key_cases.case_name: Dane County Department of Human Services v. Ponn P.
key_cases.holding: The continuing-denial-of-placement ground in Wis. Stat. sec. 48.415(4) is narrowly tailored and does not violate substantive due process on its face, because the required unfitness finding rests on the cumulative effect of the earlier judicial determinations that must precede it; a parent who pled no contest and never contested the underlying order could not mount an as-applied challenge.
key_cases.relevance: It is the immediate predecessor to Brenda B. and the Wisconsin Supreme Court's statement of what a no-contest plea to TPR grounds concedes and forfeits.
key_cases.quote: It is the cumulative effect of the determinations made at each of the previous steps that causes the finding made under § 48.415(4) to amount to unfitness.

key_cases.holding: Only the last order placing a child outside the home before a TPR petition is filed must carry the written sec. 48.356(2) warning, and although the circuit court erred under sec. 48.422(3) by failing to hear testimony supporting the petition's allegations, Steven H. was not prejudiced.
key_cases.relevance: It states the evidentiary step - testimony supporting the petition's allegations - that must precede any Wisconsin termination even when the parent does not contest grounds.
key_cases.quote: We conclude that the legislature intended the circuit court to hear testimony in support of the allegations because testimony safeguards accurate fact-finding and protects the parents.
